Mackay: One thing that impresses me about Dr. Meadow is the way she understands what I talk about at a very abstract level and in a few quick sentences turns it into something direct and practical. She has done that with ideas I wrote about a few years ago, too. She has taken concepts which were part of a philosophical analysis of psychoanalysis and translated them into very practical ways of conducting research and examining issues. That is something very commendable. It's a very special skill.

Audience member: I have a question about yesterday's conference. I was wondering what you thought about the cases, and if you could discuss them in terms of motivation theory and help us understand how you see the quest for pleasure in those cases.

Meadow: Dr. Mackay, you mentioned something in your paper which fits in here: wishes and pleasure as outcomes and affects rather than drive.

Mackay: Yes, during a psychoanalysis the analyst deals with wishes, first superficial ones then increasingly deeper wishes; however these wihses are derivatives. There is no way the analyst plumbs primary motives. The primary motives are there, but we can only infer them. Freud said as much, that primary motives are so far from the surface that they are known only by inference; they are not known directly. That is not to say that primary motives are not there and not operative. Presumably they are born of a biological source and have some evolutionary function.

More on Cause, Teleology and Drive: A Reply to Phyllis Meadow and Siamak Movahedi on “The place of motivation in psychoanalysis”

Nigel Mackay D. Phil.

Nigel Mackay

New South Wales, Australia

Nigel Mackay   Senior lecturer in psychology at the University of Wollongong, New South Wales, Australia. He is author of the monograph. Motivation and Explanation: An Essay on Freud's Philosophy of Psychology, and a number of articles on philosophical and methodological issues in psychology and psychoanalysis.

The responses by Phyllis Meadow and Siamak Movahedi to my paper “The place of motivation in psychoanalysis” are of quite different kinds. Meadow is broadly sympathetic to the line that I take; Movahedi is strongly critical. As it is the nature of these replies to focus larely on rebutting criticisms, my reply to Meadow will be shorter than that to Movahedi.

However, there are two or three points in Meadow's response that I want discuss. In my paper my interest was on the form of motivation and securing its central place in psychoanalytic theory, not with actual drive manifestation in clinical settings. Her response is to take the abstract themes that I discussed and to tease out their practical implications, linking them to clinical experience. Part of my argument was that the more obvious forms of motivation, wishes, desires and so on, many of which are consciously experienced and manifest, are the derivatives of more baisc drives. There is nothing new about this. It is the classical metapsychological position.

Now, Meadow illustrates a clinical corollary of this position that the wishes encountered in the analytic session are ephemeral and their objects shift: “My experience in the long-term treatment of patients has demonstrated that wishes come and go during the course of resistance analysis” (p. 32). However, it is the deeper and more enduring motive from which the superficial, perhaps conscious, wishes derive that is the key to understanding.

The authors of The New Informants, Christopher Bollas and David sundelson, raise important issues for the professions of psychoanalysis and psychology. One important issue raised by them is the demise of a once strictly confidential private relationship by making confidential records available to insurance companies. Attempts have been made to legalize their intrusion into a previously sacred doctor/patient relationship, including private psychotherapy. It appears that economic interests of the insurance industry are overriding consumers' needs.

The authors suggest that “psychoanalysis must become an independent profession” (p. 197). The authors, however, do not have in information at their disposal about the professional efforts already made with these issues, for example, the certification of psychoanalysts in Vermont and legislation in California governing the use of the title.

The volume raises questions about whether insurers should have access to clinical information; the authors ask should insurance or government agencies have the power to dispute treatment necessity, frequency, or length?

It is a positive event for educators and mental health professionals that this classic training guide is once again available.

The book, first published in 1976, distills the ideas of the authors, who are the two preeminent thinkers in modern psychoanalysis. The presented theory behind the understanding of disorders originating in the earliest stages of human development and the treatment techniques developed to address such pathology have gained wide acceptance and use in the past decade. The therapeutic effect of constructive aggression follows naturally from the clearly elaborated extensions of Freud's theory the techniques detailed in these pages.

Meadow's revisions frame the research and creativity of Spotnitz, who, himself, traces the contributions of many post-Freudian psychoanalysts to the understanding and treatment of narcissism. Meadow, as editor, shows how Spotnitz's concepts of emotional induction, the narcissistic transference and the contact function informed the development of a group of specialized interventions for the preverbally regressed patient. Her own body of clinical reserch and theoretical integration are especially evident in the update of her chapter on dreams. Her addition in this volume also provide the historical context for the original collacborative text and enliven it with ongoing contemporary issues.

In the first theoretical section of the book, Meadow has updated and footnoted the title of the fourth chapter, “Toward an understanding of emotional contagion.” She tells us that the chapter spans Spotnitz's thinking on the subject from 1949 through his 1970s lectures on subjective and objective countertransference.

Introduction to the Papers of Phyllis W. Meadow on Treatment Issues

Mimi Crowell PHD

Mimi Crowell

Mimi Crowell   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. She is a training analyst, supervisor, and faculty member as well as Dean of Curriculum at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. She serves on the Editorial Board of Modern Psychoanalysis.

The papers included in this section were written to help answer questions that the practitioner may often ask himself when utilizing the analytic method to deal with a variety of treatment issues. Written over the course of twenty years, Meadow has generously shared with us her thinking process on a number of difficult issues.

In her paper on “Treatment Beginnings,” Meadow demonstrates how in the first session or or first contact with the analyst, the process begins that creates the opportunity for change. As in all her other articles on treatment issues, she stresses the importance of staying with the patient in his perceptions and his projections. Maintaining defenses for as long as the patient needs them is a goal in helping the patient to ultimately be able to engage in emotional communication. Meadow warns us that in the early phase of treatment, the analyst runs the risk of unconscious manipulation of the transference out of the analyst's own needs or unconscious inductions to repeat the patient's past, thus not allowing the patient to develop the kind of narcissistic transference he needs. We must be able to feel all of our own feelings with our patients and resonate with them, so that they can say anything to us or hear anything from us.

One of the themes that emerge from these papers and continues to be clarified in all her writing is the belief that the analyst should not limit herself to any one mode of thought or way of working.

The psychoanalytic method was first developed as a procedure for gathering data on intrapsychic functioning both within a human system and in the interaction of systems with each other. Skill in the procedure was learned within the framework of regular meetings between patient and analyst, at a fixed time, place and fee. Analytic candidates were taught to study the forces interfering with spontaneous communication within the analytic session and to learn to intervene to resolve blocks to communication.

Because the psychoanalytic method of investigation constitutes a natural experiment in which psychic events occur repetitively, it is difficult to separate research from practice. Psychoanalytic practice was and is the setting in which conclusions about emotional and mental functioning are drawn and made explicit. According to Shepherd (1982), “Each patient the candidate treats is a subject of research into the unique patterning of instinctual forces that comprise that individual as well as a representative of the general laws governing psychic functioning.”

Candidates training to be psychoanalysts begin their training by working on their observational skills in the classroom, in supervision of case work, and in case conferences. They are taught to use the analytic session to make increasingly more accurate observations and to recognize their own biases.

Phyllis Meadow PHD

Phyllis Meadow

As researchers were pointing out as early as 1962, the major problem for psychoanalysis, if it intends to qualify as a reputable science, lies in its ability to develop its own method for observing events.

In the early sixties when I was beginning to think about writing a dissertation at New York University, arguments abounded against the possibility of confirming psychoanalytic concepts. Logical positivism still dominated the thinking of social scientists. This was an approach to research that viewed truth as absolute rather than as relative to … or a function of …. Positivists sought answers to questions concerning causation. In its attempt to reach directly from the observed to the infinite, logical positivism declared theoretical concepts useless. In its methodology it adopted quantitative inductivism, the theory that operated on the assumption that the larger the number of examples provided, the greater the proof. A review of the literature of that day demonstrates that counting did not lead to new insights, but both groups continued to criticize the psychoanalytic research then in vogue.

Edelson (1984), a psychoanalyst and philosopher of science, summed up the fallacy of quantitative inductivism—the theory that the greater the number of persons observed, the greater the degree of support for an hypothesis—stating as an example of this thinking an investigation of the relationship between homosexuality and paranoia.

*Paper originally published in Mod. Psychoanal. Vol. 17, No. 2, 1992.335

Madonna has produced a videotape called “Truth or Dare,” which epitomizes negative union. It tells the sad story of a bright and talented woman who cannot form relations, whose life on stage is her only life. It shows the way she clings to, and even takes over, the lives of the people who work for her. It illustrates how she fights off isolation with sexual and body contact, desperately seeking a connection as she play-acts roles. It ends with her theme song, “Keep people together forever and ever, people together ever and ever.” Madonna created a world for herself and lives in it fully, playing at union.

What would happen to Madonna if she brought her conflicts to a modern analyst? She has found a way to live her longings in a fantasy of connectedness. While her unhappiness finds some abatement in action, she cannot achieve permanent relief. If Madonna were in treatment the analyst would not have the task of working through the defenses against the arousal of early longings, but might have difficulty helping her to verbalize longings in the transference because action provides a partial outlet for longings.

In this paper, I would like to describe what happens to primitive emotions freed from the self-destructive solutions of the narcissistic defense over long-term treatment, in the course of which the narcissistic defenses have been worked through and distancing mechanisms have been replaced by emotional expression.

Deborah Margolis is not on a Freud bashing expedition nor is she engaged in political edealization. Rather she takes us on a journey guided by Freud's idea that our complexes are sources of our weaknesses and our strengths. Although Freud actively sought to lead his biographers astray, Margolis's detailed knowledge of the terrain and her psychoanalytically trained perspective directs us to a fascinating exploration of “Freud's preoedipal complexes which have so richly endowed our civilization.”

Deborah Margolis has crafted more than a book about Freud and his mother. The subtitle, Preoedipal Aspects of Freud's Personality, more accurately describes the scope of the work. Margolis introduces us to mother Amalia and her family of origin. We find ourselves in the home of Amalia and Jacob Freud, observing the family interactions.

The question of whether psychoanalysis is a science has troubled its critics since its inception. Freud considered psychoanalysis to be a science. However some critics complain that psychoanalytic theories cannot be tested, that it doesn't conform to the scientific method or the statistical and quantitative studies popular among the social sciences, that the observer is a participant. Meadow has long been intimately involved with psychoanalytic research as it concerns the theory, practice and education of candidates-in-training.

In her early paper, “A Research Method for Investigating the Effectiveness of Psychoanalytic Techniques,” not reprinted here, Meadow followed a quantitative model. She designed an experimental approach that allowed her to measure the efficacy of interventions. The study is replete with scales and statistics, tables and numbers. A conclusion is reached. She has since moved away from such research designs. Psychoanalysis is not a hard science nor a social science. It cannot control and isolate variables; it cannot manipulate environment. Psychoanalysis lives within a unique set of assumptions from which it proceeds, for example, the presence of a dynamic unconscious that influences behavior. Its basic assumptions are not questioned. From them, the discourse of psychoanalysis emerges. And like Freud, Meadow's thinking on research has evolved and will continue to evolve as her commitment to research impels her toward the frontier.

I don't know many people who will agree with my ideas but that's probably because not many impulisives have the itme to write. Debates over whether the single case study can provide a scientific method have not yet been resolved. While the usefulness of the theory of the unconscious has not been seriously questioned, philosophers of science and many psychoanalysts have criticized claims that the past can be reliably reconstructed from transference or, more important, that we can demonstrate our core constructs (Grunbaum, 1993).

This essay will not argue with this point. I will not consider research based on a reconstruction of the past or studies of the effectiveness of psychoanalytic treatment based on outcomes.

The questions tobe considered in this paper are: Can we reliably examine events in the psychoanalytic session? In thinking about severe emotinal illness, modern analysts have come to view the solutions patients use to deal with their emotional conflicts to be variations on patterns of turning destructive impulses inward. It helps if we view these solutions as organized mental activity in which the flow of energy can be understood as a method for mastering tension. Using object language to think about the regressed patient is usually an error. Pleasure-pain, tension reduction, overstimulation are terms which better fit the longings and rage with which the narcissistic patient is struggling. Drive theory provides us with the picture of conflict as an insufficient quantity of libido in the system to cope with the amount of tension.

It is clear in a reading of the psychoanalytic literature that despite our experience of treatment with the regressed aspects of a patient, thinking in drive theory terms is difficult for the analyst. When writing, we tend to convert phenomenological experience into self-object representations. When the feeling in the room with a patient is of vast spaces, we describe it as aloneness or emptiness. This is understandable since no psyche stood still at the periods we are capturing. Layers of pre-object and object experience are added to the surviving psyche. But the period of life experienced in psychosis returns to a pre-object state, and for the most part, a pre self-object merged state. Much of the experience recaptured in sessions dates to a dawning awareness of being and a responsiveness to that awareness of existence.

Before I address the issue of transference, I would like to say something about modern psychoanalysis. The word modern modifying psychoanalysis sounds presumptuous to me since within each school of thought, modern ideas emerge out of existing theory. The problem of the modern-day therapist is the same as that of Freud who wrote, “The task of psychoanalysis is to help the patient say everything.” From this simple explanation of the analyst's mission two problems have emerged.

When the analyst asks the patient to talk, the patient develops a resistance to doing so. Freud was the first to discover this. He wrote that one hardly comes across a patient who does not attempt to reserve a region of himself for himself and to prevent treatment from touching that area. It is this activity that analysts refer to when they say the patient is resistant. Today's challenge, the narcissistic disorders, present even more difficulties for the talking cure. Narcissistic patients present us with nonverbal, symbolic communications or actions to express themselves, because they do not have the language with which to describe their conflicts.

A second discovery made by analysts was that, like patients, they do not want to hear everything, particularly those things that might wound the therapist's ego. The problem for therapists is that if the patient says everything it may arouse in the therapist very painful feelings and impulses. These, then, are the two main interferences to bringing about change through psychoanalysis.

Commentators are generally agreed that psychoanalysis is a theory of motivation. However, there is controversy over what is the motivational essence of the theory and, relatedly, on how motivation itself should be conceptualized. One common solution to these issues is to treat the commonsense form of explanation, that of appealing to wishes and beliefs to explain action, as the model for psychoanalytic explanation and, at the same time, to reject causal drive accounts of motive like Freud's. This solution retains motivation's central place in psychoanalysis, but depicts the person as by nature a striver toward goals. However, as long as the concept of wish (or motive) is merely that of something defined in terms of its goals or objects, or constituted by its relation to such objects, then it is not anything in itself, it is incoherent, and wish explanations are only teleological pseudo-explanations, inadequate for psychoanalysis. Freud's drive theory, whatever its theoretical problems, provides an account of motivation that is free of these metatheoretical difficulties. It treats motives as drives and drives as processes defined by source and not by object. It offers an account of how objects are learned to be instrumental in regulating drive processes and how wishes derive from more basic motive states. In doing this, Freud's drive theory is a candidate for a coherent and proper explanation of motivation.

In 1976 two books were published, one by Hyman Spotnitz, Psychotherapy of Preoedipal Conditions, and one by Hyman Spotnitz and Phyllis W. Meadow, Treatment of the Narcissistic Neuroses. The debate over whether psychoanalysis is a branch of natural science or whether it is a hermeneutic endeavor currently divides the psychoanalytic community. One view, held by writers like Mackay (1989), Meadow (1992, 1995), and Brenner (1980), is that psychoanalysis is, as Freud always insisted, a scientific discipline whose findings are, in principle at least, verifiable empirically. Opposing this view is the position held by Gill (1976, 1978), Schafer (1976, 1983), Steele (1979), and others, which maintains that psychoanalysis is not amenable to the research methodology of empirical science, and that it is really a hermeneutic discipline concerned with intentionality and meaning rather than causation. The conflict between these two opposing factions has taken on a rigid, “either-or” complexion which threatens the integrity of psychoanalysis more than does any outside criticism. Both strains—the hermeneutic and the natural scientific—can be found in Freud's work. Indeed, this breadth and complexity is a hallmark of Freud's writing, and bespeaks an awareness on Freud's part that psychoanalysis is both Naturwissenschaft and Geisteswissenschaft. The polarization of attitudes in the debate over what kind of discipline psychoanalysis really is has led to infighting which is unnecessary and harmful to the field, and which deprives each side of the enrichment of the insights of the other.

While praising Nigel Mackay's scholarly paper, I have taken issue with some of his conclusions. I have argued that his rejection of purposive explanations is based on a confusion between the teleological language and teleological system. I have expressed much doubt about the adequacy of his reductionistic proposal of dispensing with wishes, intentions, beliefs and meanings in favor of the physical state of the organism. I have contended that as psychoanalysts we are not interested in explaining the movements of the body. We are rather interested in understanding their meanings in the psychoanalytic situation. And from knowing the physical states of the organism associated with movements of the body, we cannot decipher their meanings. I have also argued that reductions in terms of ad hoc definitions are simply tautological exercises that might render different ways of describing a process or an event. A recast of a clinical phenomenon in terms of drives rather than wish or belief, is neither a lawful reduction nor an “unpacking.” It is simply a re-packing, merely changing the language of a particular narrative.

A single man who wanted to work with a woman so he could be prepared for marriage entered one of my groups ten years ago. He said he wanted to learn to express anger. During the first sessions he seemed to express nothing else. He complained about what was said and he ranted about what was not said. He spoke of the group members as wrong and stupid and of the analyst as the worst of all. Group members were puzzled by his repetitiveness, but when they asked about this venting of spleen, he expressed surprise. “What else would a successful group member do?” Within several weeks he recognized that other kinds of communication were taking place in the group. Not clear about the difference he said, “I thought that I was fluent in self-expression, but you people speak a whole new dialect.”

Like this man, many people come to group with preconceived notions. Some think that it's for people who are shy or need help in socializing. Analytic candidates may come to round out their training. Others believe they may not be ready for group; they say they don't experience a sense of family, or of brothers and sisters being emotionally real. One patient said, “My father doesn't really exist inside me; he is just an idea.”

The initial sessions with a psychoanalytic patient make evident the rationale for the particular style each analyst has of entering a relationship with a patient. For my part, when I begin an analysis, I pay attention to the simplest concerns. For example, the room should be pleasant, neither too warm nor too cool, neither too welllit nor too dim. My style of dress is usually not extreme, nor does it attract too much of the patient's attention. I want to enter the session relaxed, that is, free enough of distractions so that I can be interested in what the patient wants to talk about. However, I don't want to be overly interested-I don't want to lean forward in my seat or hang on the person's every word. In the first session my primary interest is in why the patient is consulting me. To find out more about the problem I ask some variation on the question, “What brings you here?” It is not my intention to say much more in the early part of this session unless the patient addresses me directly with questions, or a question is necessary to make sense out of what my visitor is saying.

I find that when I act like this in the first session my visitor responds in his own style to my question “Why are you here?” He may or may not ask questions.
